Senses.Explanation: The components mean “biased or tilted” (偏), “within” (中), and “upright or straight” (正): "the upright within the biased." It is the second of the (五位) (Five Ranks) of (洞山良价) (Dongshan Liangjie), whose (五位君臣頌) gives it: (偏中正)，(失曉老婆逢古鏡)。(分明覿面別無真)，(休更迷頭猶認影). (曹山本寂) (Caoshan Benji), asked the (五位君臣旨訣), supplies the corpus's own definition: (正位即空界)，(本來無物)。(偏位即色界)，(有萬象形)。(正中偏者)，(背理就事)。(偏中正者)，(舍事入理) — i.e. "(偏中正): setting aside affairs and entering into principle" (偏中正者，舍事入理), the exact inverse of (正中偏者)，(背理就事). In his ruler-minister scheme (君為正位，臣為偏位) he assigns it: "the minister facing the ruler is (偏中正)" (臣向君是偏中正). It is deployed as a stock test-question — (如何是偏中正)？ — answered with a turning phrase (宏智正覺: 師曰：白髮老婆羞看鏡). A later sermon maps the ranks onto Linji-school terms (以濟宗論之): (正中偏奪人也)，(偏中正奪境也). Beyond the graphs and these attested self-definitions the texts add no further gloss, and neither does this entry.
Senses.Note: The verse is (洞山良价)'s (五位君臣頌); the (舍事入理) / (空界)·(色界) / (君臣) definitions are (曹山本寂)'s, given in answer to (五位君臣旨訣) — do not cross-attribute the verse and the gloss. Both are witnessed across ≥2 independent lamp records (禪宗正脉 X85n1593, 五燈全書 X81n1571) AND in the masters' own recorded sayings: the verse in (瑞州洞山良价禪師語錄) (T47n1986B), the (旨訣) answer in (撫州曹山元證禪師語錄) (T47n1987A). Pairs with and inverts (正中偏) (舍事入理 vs 背理就事; 臣向君 vs 君視臣). Member of the Five Ranks (五位) with (正中偏) · (正中來) · (兼中至) · (兼中到).

Senses.Explanation: Literally "question and answer" (問答). In Chan records it names the spoken exchange itself, a recurring division of masters' records, and a component of the compound "question-and-answer encounters" (問答機緣). Zhaozhou is asked how he responds when every question-and-answer falls in the thinking faculty; he answers, "Ask" (問), so the record places the term inside an enacted exchange. Zhongfeng describes question and answer "racing across one another" (問答交馳), with the question in the answer and the answer in the question. Other records preserve headings for question-and-answer, pair it with requests for instruction, entry into the room, and examination, or state "question-and-answer was not recorded" (問答不錄) before retaining the subsequent address.
Senses.Note: The corpus does not treat the label as sufficient by itself. One record objects that "recently many take question-and-answer to be Chan" (近世多以問答為禪) and says the houses' styles thereby become unclear. Another master raises the whisk and says, "set question-and-answer encounters aside" (機緣問答且置), then asks whether the assembly understands the whisk. These are attested restrictions on equating a recorded format with Chan; they do not remove public questioning from the records. Family check: "a monk asked" (僧問) is the speaker-turn formula; "request instruction" (請益) names a request for instruction; "enter the room" (入室) identifies admission or entry; "supply a phrase" (下語) names supplying a phrase or judgment. "Question-and-answer" (問答) names the reciprocal exchange and does not replace those narrower terms. The headword has 1,242 occurrences in 244 allowlisted texts.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “ask words”: to put a question in an encounter, and by extension the questioning or the person who does it. The public role is grammatical and institutional in the records: a master calls, “is there anyone with a question? Quickly bring the question forward” (更有問話者麼，速致問來), or “let anyone who knows how to question come forward” (有解問話者出來). Monks compete to step out and question during an ascending-the-hall address, and another record calls a participant “the monk who asked the question” (問話僧). The corpus also examines the quality of questioning. An essay titled “Warning on Questioning” says recent questioning attracts criticism because people do not know the purpose of “putting forward a question, presenting a doubt, and requesting instruction” (伸問、致疑、咨請), and instead use congratulatory and seasonal phrases. Deshan's recorded “tonight I will not answer; anyone who questions gets thirty blows” still produces a monk who steps forward, and later records repeatedly raise and comment on that encounter. The term thus names an exposed speaking turn open to answer, refusal, rebuke, or later appraisal; it does not guarantee a successful or approved question.
Senses.Note: Allowlist count: 871 hits in 210 texts. Productive forms include “questioner / anyone who questions” (問話者, 274 hits / 124 texts), “questioning monk” (問話僧, 52 / 36), and “a monk came out to question” (僧出問話, attested across multiple records). The Zen bend is the term's public-interview role and the tradition's explicit scrutiny of how a question is put, not merely the ordinary verb “ask.”
